utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody and thank you, Madam Registrar. All the accused are here. I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Haynes from amongst the Defence teams. Prosecution, I see Mr. Haynes -- Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Nicholls, who is accompanied by the expert who is assisting the Prosecution or who will be assisting the Prosecution during the testimony of the Defence expert. Mr. Thayer, could you please introduce your expert? Mr. Vanderpuye, sorry, Mr. Vanderpuye, could you kindly introduce your expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, good afternoon to you and Your Honours. This is Major Richard Angove and you've referred to him correctly. He will be here to observe the testimony of the Defence expert. At this point, he's a consultant with us and he's advising us concerning the testimony as well as the expert report. So I think that sufficiently introduces him if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. How does he spell his name? I'm asking how does he, because I'm not quite sure that you would spell it right, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A-N-G-O-V-E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So that's it. Have you more or less come to an agreement what's going to happen with this witness? Because I feel it is very unlikely that we will finish with him today. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday and today, I spoke to Mr. Rodic concerning this delay which will quite evidently occur during his testimony. He contacted the company he works for, and he was informed that there was no possibility for him not to report for work at the start of the next week. That's to say Monday-Tuesday. Therefore, he can be here today and tomorrow, but there is no possibility for him to be absent from work on Monday. He can provide you with all the relevant details. He received a facsimile from his company. I asked him when it was that he could reappear. He was unable to provide me with an answer now but in the course of the next week, he could furnish us with a possible date for his testimony in June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you very much, Mr. Zivanovic, for that information. You are aware that we had already agreed sometime back that we will not be sitting tomorrow. I notice Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to complicate the matter further, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. To assist in clarifying the issue a bit, if I may, Your Honour, it is an important witness. It's a Defence expert witness on the intercept project. It is going to take, just the direct, in excess of I believe or as we estimate, four hours to do it. We don't believe we could even complete the direct today. We would propose, as we've suggested to my learned friend, friends from the Office of the Prosecution, that the witness start and end in a specific period and we are contemplating or trying to determine from him if he can come immediately after the recess during the week of June 11th or actually the 12th, on Tuesday, when we reconvene as opposed to starting him and then concluding him later. And the reason we suggest that is because then we would not have any contact with him for over or close to a month's period of time and it would be necessary to continue to draw out certain questions that other Defence attorneys may have on specific intercepts, although he's generally giving the Court an overview of the capacity of those intercepted or purported intercepted conversations. So we proposed to the Prosecution, and they didn't seem to have an objection to it, although I wasn't 100 per cent clear on their position, that the witness, in fact, start in mid-June at the convenience of the Court, the Prosecution and the witness, so that we have him in one block period of a two or three-day session, so that was something we would propose to the Court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before -- before or after PW-108?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the Court's ruling, given our motion and our replies to that motion. We would be at the Court's discretion as to how the Court wants to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The other point I failed to mention which I should, Your Honour, and that is with respect to Mr. Rodic, the expert, we believe he has been, quite candidly, inconvenienced to a certain degree. Although he's assisting us, he's been waiting for several days now and he's quite anxious to get back and has the demands of his employer which we can't control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were talking about that this morning in Chambers, because as you know, we do have at heart a lot of concern about witnesses that come here to testify, and it's something that worries us. So what's your position, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, everyone. Let me be 100 per cent clear on the Prosecution's position. We are prepared to proceed today. We have been prepared to do so pursuant to the schedule we've had. We have our consultant here. He is ready. I don't see any reason to postpone this witness's direct testimony until some further date. What we have done in the past with witnesses is to bring them back for cross-examination. As I understand it, Mr. Rodic has been here since at least the 17th. If Defence counsel needed time to coordinate their examinations, they had ample opportunity to do so. I do not believe that this change in the date on which his testimony is set to proceed warrants postponing his direct testimony any further. We are ready to go. We do not have any witnesses available to fill the time today because we have been aiming for sometime to try to get this completed. So our position is quite clear. We are ready. I understand that the Defence counsel is ready to present this direct testimony. We see no good reason to postpone this testimony any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is the first time we've heard that their position is clear on this point but let me make it very clear. The Defence doesn't need additional time to prepare this expert. He has his report. The report's been submitted. It's been submitted in due time which their expert can refer to. I just want to make for the record an observation that even though at times the Court has restricted me from extending some cross-examination questions and even at the objection of my learned friends a couple times they projected that I went over a specified time limit, we've seen in the last two, three days, as the Court has mentioned, it's the OTP and specifically my learned friend Mr. Thayer that extended, as I think the Court said on the record yesterday, three times their estimate. This is not our fault. They extended it. We plead leave for obviously different reasons than from what they claim. We think it's necessary that the expert be shown to the Court in one full period, whether it's two or four days' sessions, and that is most convenient for the Court and all the parties to commence in July, given his schedule that he cannot return next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My only question to you is this: That originally, it was projected that there will be two hours from -- by Mr. Zivanovic and then another hour between the Beara and the Nikolic teams, plus one hour the Borovcanin -- 15 minutes, sorry, the Borovcanin team. We had suggested that there should only be one examination-in-chief and then obviously if there are any leftovers, they will be catered for. How come that we have now got four hours plus? Can't we start and finish in three hours, can't we start and finish the examination-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we can, Your Honour. It's not something that's orchestrated as tightly as the Prosecution's witnesses, but we think it may take longer and given the estimates by other counsel from the Defence who are not using this witness as a joint expert, we estimate generally that it may take in excess of four hours, given those time periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But our idea was once the direct is finished, cross-examination goes to the Prosecution and then if there is Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic who would like to cross-examine this witness, he -- they will come after the Prosecution and not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I included their time, Your Honour, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Ostojic. Shall we start and try and finish with this witness and then he can come for cross-examination when it's most convenient for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If that's the Court's ruling, of course we will abide by it, Your Honour. We do have other housekeeping matters we can deal with but if the Court wants to put that off, we shall do as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure the housekeeping matters won't engage us for three hours, so they seem very complicated in your mind. So let's proceed. Shall we proceed, Judge Prost? Okay. So we are going to proceed. For the record we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today, Judge Stole couldn't be with us for personal reasons, compelling personal reasons, so, yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we continue sitting today and proceed with the examination-in-chief, I wanted to raise the matter of our contacts with the expert witness in the meantime. I have to inform you that we've been dealing with a number of technical difficulties, and we shall have to be in touch with him in the case there is a break between today's examination-in-chief and the Prosecution's cross-examination. In view of that proceeding now will place us in a very difficult situation because we will not be able to work with him on other matters that we have engaged him for in this case. For this reason, we would find it quite appropriate to deal with his testimony at a later stage so that in the meantime we could make use of his other services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is none of our concern, Mr. Zivanovic. What is of our concern is that for all intents and purposes, this person was supposed to come here yesterday, start yesterday or the day before, and finish with his testimony. So let's not talk about further consultations with him in relation to what he's going to testify upon now. Other matters, I don't think we even need to discuss them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically to make it clear, if he doesn't finish the testimony today, there is no reason why -- on earth why we should allow you to approach the witness to make or to further -- make further consultations -- have further consultations with him on the subject of his testimony today, but on other matters you only have to ask and we will grant you so, like we have granted on previous occasions. In other words, if it there are other matters that you have engaged this witness upon which he is not going to testify upon now, today, or later on, if he doesn't finish his testimony today, then of course you can have consultations with him but not on what he is going to testify today and when he finishes this part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We think that's a fair approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've done it in the past even with your own witnesses, so let's proceed. Madam Usher, could you kindly bring the witness in? I just want a confirmation from both sides that the tendering of documents relating to Mr. Trivic's testimony will be dealt with at a later stage, sometime next week. Is that agreed? That's what has been communicated to you as the express desire and wish of the parties. Confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's confirmed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is, Mr. Josse, I may have given you the impression that after he finishes the direct examination, Prosecution will go on cross-examination first. Actually, the decision is in the inverse. You will go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We had rather assumed that, Your Honour. It may be that we should have a brief discussion at some point about this because of course we are in the very unusual situation of a Defence witness giving evidence in the middle of a Prosecution case. Normally this is a matter I suspect we would have explored at a Pre-Defence Conference pursuant to the rules, so there may be one or two procedural matters that we should iron out as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. But you -- or Mr. Josse that we had discussed very briefly this matter of having evidence brought forward by the Defence during the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you were free to either decide to bring such evidence forward or not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour says that this is in no way a precedent to what's going to happen in the Defence case, then we are quite content to cross-examine before the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a precedent. You can take it as definitely in the affirmative. It's not a precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, you were free to -- each one of you was free not to adopt --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed we could have objected to this course. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been brought here by some of the Defence teams as their expert on matters related to interception of radio relay communications and you're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read it out aloud and that will be your commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, take a seat. Mr. Zivanovic, who is lead counsel, Defence team appearing for Colonel Popovic, Vujadin Popovic, will be examining you in chief. Please try to keep your answers as brief as possible, and try to be to the point as much as you can. Mr. Zivanovic. If you wish to ask the witness what his position is in relation to his employer and overstaying past the weekend, maybe here Monday when we hope to finish with his witness you're free to do so rather than put the questions myself. I'm saying this because you hinted that he may wish to make statements in this regard. Anyway, unless you prefer to go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I explained the reasons why Mr. Rodic is not able to stay on in The Hague, so I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: My name is Djuro Rodic, son of Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 6th of May, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Strmica, near Knin, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What schooling do you have?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the Electrical Engineering College, the special -- and I specialised in telecommunications. I completed the course in Split, which is attached to the Zagreb University.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any specialisation courses or any additional advancement courses related to your profession?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I had been working for 30 years in the army of Yugoslavia, between 1973 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 83 and 2003.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: -- I had to undergo training. I am a radio relay officer by specialisation and it was with the company ISKRA in Ljubljana that I attended courses for multiplexing equipment that had been manufactured there. This was early on in my career. I went on to attend specialisation courses in Munich, in their telecommunications centre for multiplexing equipment as well as in their institute and factory for manufacturing radio relay devices for military purposes. I also attended specialisation courses with the institute for microwave technology in Belgrade. I continually attended courses within the school centre for communications attached to the VJ General Staff. In addition to these courses, I took part in a number of training for dealing with radio relay stations and terminal radio relay stations. At the end of my military career, in order to continue working, I felt young, I had to take the exam, the professional exam, with the Chamber of Engineering in Belgrade in order to be licensed to work as project manager of telecommunications systems and networks, and that's what I'm doing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've mentioned that in your CV. You told us that you worked for 30 years in the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the army of Yugoslavia, or rather, in that same force which changed name over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the period that you attended your active service in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Rodic, you need to allow a short interval between question and answer because you are rendering the interpreter's life miserable. I can sense the stress they are experiencing in trying to catch up with both of you, who speak the same language, so please allow a short pause. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know I will be back saying the same thing in about two minutes' time, but in the meantime please try.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly what your service in the army of Yugoslavia was throughout your military career there until your retirement?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As I joined the army as an active serviceman, I started in the group for radio relay communications of the armed forces and in setting up radio relay networks, which included supervision of the construction of the network, checks of the system, measurements concerning that particular system, and carrying out the interconnection of various networks so that they could be of service to the armed forces. As I gained experience, I continued working in efforts to perfect the existing radio relay systems and networks and to define the requirements for further development and production of such equipment of a new generation, of cutting edge equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: As the equipment was being used by the army, I set up experimental networks and took part in gradual assimilation of this equipment into the army life. At a later stage, I worked on the procurement of communications devices for the purposes of the army. As I was setting up radio relay networks, I also examined the flow of data and the functioning of the radio relay systems across borders, and I mean across borders with neighbouring countries. This was very important because we had to make sure that the flow of data was kept at the minimum so that the neighbouring countries would not raise their complaints about interference from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you joined the armed forces and when you retired?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: It was on the 1st of November, 1973 that I joined the army, and my service was terminated at the end of October, 2003, on which date I had completed the full 30 years of service for the armed forces of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In time of war in the former Yugoslavia, where did you serve? And I'm referring to the period between 1991 and the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I spent the entire period in one institute and that was the communications administration with the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. I have to say that the -- at the end of December.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: At the end of September --

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: 1992, up until the end of March, 1993, when my native area was under threat, I went and joined the army of Republika Srpska and I defended my people during the aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time, in which town?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The seat of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was in Knin, and I spent six months in that town in the headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you continue your service then after the month of March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I went back to where I had originally come from when I came to Knin. I went to the communications administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which time was that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, after Ljubljana and then Montenegro, I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From that period on, until the end of the war, did you ever go to the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I went there twice, in the aftermath of the bombing of Veliki Zep when the radio relay path, 120-channel path, active between Cer and Veliki Zep was destroyed. I was an expert and in charge of restoring that radio relay path into working order. The second time was in mid-August, 1995, when as part of the assistance to the army of Republika Srpska, I toured all their radio relay nodes and all the most important radio relay stations, terminal radio relay stations, in order to make sure that the system which was in quite a poor condition was upgraded as far as it was possible, given the resources we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this: When did your first visit to Veliki Zep take place? You said when the second time took place but can you tell us about the first time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That was a year earlier. I think it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my next question: You told us that in 1994 and 1995, you were discharging the services you described. These were regular duties within your profession?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I was a specialist in that area and there weren't many people who were capable of seeing that work through. I believe that we spent two days at that particular facility each time we visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these jobs you performed, did you also perform any other jobs that were outside your line of profession? And I'm referring to the territory Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No. I was lucky enough that I was able to remain within the bounds of my profession throughout my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the work of some commissions or delegations that dealt with disarmament and arms control and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No, never, in that territory or in any other territory, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in touch with any paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No. I strictly adhered to the military ethics and professional ethics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, can you tell us briefly what the task was with regard to your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The task of my expert report, in my understanding, was to assess the possibility of interception of radio communications of the army of Republika Srpska along radio relay paths of Vlasenica-Veliki Zep-Cer-Gucevo and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the reason for choosing that particular route?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Because according to the diagram of the radio communications of the Drina Corps, it was along that route that radio relay communications took part of the Drina Corps, which was headquartered in Vlasenica. Their communications with the Zvornik Brigade and Bratunac Brigade. Moreover, communications could be set with the superior command or, rather, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it along that route of Vlasenica-Veliki Zep-Cer-Gucevo-Zvornik, that all radio relay communications of the Drina Corps and the units you just mentioned were transmitted?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were along that same route radio relay communications by RU-800 and RU 1 carried out? Or was it with only one of them?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, they used only one of them because they did not use both for that particular route.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Were radio relay communications transmitted along that route with RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Not along that route but on the route from Veliki Zep to Bratunac, yes, it was along that route that RRU-1 maintained communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were radio relay communications carried out by radio relay device RRU-1 the subject of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That was my wish, but I was unable to obtain the necessary data in order to analyse communications carried out through the RRU-1 device. So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On this route, in addition to the communications by RRU-1 and RRU-800 devices, were any other devices used for communication?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: On the first path, Vlasenica-Veliki Zep-Cer-Gucevo-Zvornik. On the part of the route between Veliki Zep and Cer, radio relay communications were carried out with another type of device, which was SMC 1306 B. That was the type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These devices, SMC 1306 B, did you analyse them?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Because the documentation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina shows that they did not intercept any communications through this device, but only communications through RRU-1 and RRU-800. Apart from this, an inspection of their listening-in equipment led me to conclude that they were unable to intercept any communications carried out by SMC 1306 B because they were -- they did not have any equipment operating on the 55 gigahertz range.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now explain to us the difference between the RRU-1 and RRU-800 devices, briefly?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, to put it simply, RRU is a one channel or single channel radio relay device operating in a frequency range of 235 to 270 megahertz. It's an analog device. RRU-800 is a multi-channel radio relay device with a capacity of four or 12 or 24 telephone channels, and for this it needs the support of a multiplex device and it operates in a frequency range of 610 to 960 megahertz. In addition to these differences, they resemble one another because they are radio relay devices used to direct point-to-point communication. They differ in their manner of use. The one channel, single channel radio relay device, which contains a multiplex part is intended for lower level tactical units. It's portable. It can be carried by a single soldier. It can be used for quick communication. Whereas RRU-800 is more intended for a stationary radio relay system and that was how it was used for the most part in the radio relay network.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what conditions are required in order to intercept communications done through RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, there are several prerequisites as follows: First, the person wishing to intercept the communication needs equipment. Secondly, that person has to position his equipment in suitable sites. Thirdly, an organisation and experts are required. And lastly -- last but not least-- the frequencies have to match when listening in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the frequencies have to match, you mean the frequency used by the person intercepting and --

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, intercepting or listening in is carried out as follows. A transmitter transmits a signal on a certain frequency. The person intercepting has to adjust his equipment to that frequency, that precise frequency, in order to be able to listen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me what kind of equipment is needed to intercept communications using RRU-800 for the communication?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't use just any kind of intercepting equipment. It has to be suitable to the frequency range it is intended for. In order to intercept a signal emitted by RRU-800, the receiver used to intercept the communication has to have a frequency range covering the frequency range of this piece of equipment. Furthermore, its sensitivity, the sensitivity of the receiver has to be such that the signal is of good quality and that it can be received reliably. What is very important is the antenna system, which has to be suitable for the frequency range of the devices being listened into. It must be oriented well because this will improve the quality significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had such equipment?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: From what I have been able to ascertain through the documentation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in their north and south sites, they had amateur equipment of the 1990 generation, which they were able to obtain. As a rule, they were able to intercept RRU-1 and RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to explain to the Chamber, I told the witness not to mention the names of the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but to refer to them as north and south, which is why the witness used this terminology. Out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for that. Actually, the moment he said the north and the south side, we immediately noticed that there was some direction, good direction, in this case. So our gratitude for that, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the impact of the position of the radio sets used to intercept on the intercepting process itself?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Well, the location is very important for the possibility of interception. It should be as close as possible to the devices being listened to, and not only close in terms of distance but also the position should be such that as many devices as possible can be listened to under favourable angles in relation to the angles of the radio relay communication and the orientation of the antenna of the radio relay devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify a certain point, when you say the devices being listened to, are you referring to the five that you listed in your schema of radio relay communications?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I refer exclusively to those five facilities that are -- I analysed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I put this question was to avoid misunderstanding because someone might think we might be referring to somebody using a telephone or something like that. That's why I put this question to you, although I knew what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: By your leave, I will clarify further. When I say "the facility being listened to," those are the radio relay facilities and stations on the route that I mentioned, and if we want to go into detail, those are the antennae on those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly what the distance was of the -- of the interception stations of the north and south positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Gucevo and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: In my analysis, that is in addendum number 10, and as it's quite some distance, I will use that addendum or appendix. Interception station North 8 was 72.9 kilometres away from Cer. Crni Vrh, 52.7 kilometres. Zvornik, 53.7 kilometres. Veliki Zep, 79.3 kilometres. Vlasenica, 64.9 kilometres. From the interception station south, Zvornik is 47.1 kilometres away, and Crni Vrh, 54.4 kilometres. Cer, 82.7 kilometres. Veliki Zep, 46.9 kilometres, and Vlasenica, 34.2 kilometres. According to the topographical maps, those are the distances. In brief, then, we have 30 or more kilometres, up to 80 kilometres' distance. From the standpoint of distance, those are the figures. Some of these longer paths were not favourable, and in the calculations one can see the influence of distance on the suppression of the electromagnetic wave reaching the antenna of the interception equipment from the station emitting the signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in general, whether intercepting at these distances is possible with the intercepting devices at the disposal of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in general?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: There are three types of devices according to the documentation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, as a rule, were able to be used to intercept communications in these locations under certain conditions. It's not just the equipment but also the antennae and the orientation and whether or not there is optical visibility. So all these can have an influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the effect is of the elevation above sea level on the possibilities of listening in?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The elevation above sea level influences the quality and possibility of intercepting because the intercepting station, which is higher up, has better optical and radio visibility in relation to the facilities intercepted, but visibility is not always there because that depends on what there is between those two points, whether there are hills, valleys, and so on. So it also depends on the geographical features between those two points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify this, can you tell us what you mean by optical visibility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Optical visibility between the intercepting station or antenna and the antenna of the radio relay device means that when one looks at the land profile and the curves of the land, there are no obstacles along that route, so that if one were able to see with the naked eye, one would have to be able to stand at the elevation where the intercepting device is and see the antenna of the radio relay device broadcasting the signal. Did you ask me about radio visibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, only about optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Explain what radio visibility is.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That is an even stricter criterion, because the spreading of electro-magnetic waves does not take place only along a single line. It has to go through a wider area which has to be free in order for reception to be of high quality, and I have explained this in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us at what point above sea level the intercepting stations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in the north and south location?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: In the northern location, it was at 815 metres above sea level, which is not a very favourable height. On the southern location, it was 1326 metres, which is somewhat more favourable, in terms of intercepting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What were your findings in relation to the visibility of Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Gucevo and Zvornik facilities from the intercepting stations north and south?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I examined this on the basis of topographical military maps, as I had done in my military career, and the findings are in appendices 20 to 29. In item 7, I gave a comment, an explanation, of these findings in relation to each of these facilities as to whether there was visibility or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was visibility an interference or was it an obstacle to the intercepting activities along the mentioned radio relay route?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: According to my calculations, in view of optical and radio visibility or because of optical and radio visibility, the Vlasenica- Veliki Zep path could not be intercepted because Vlasenica does not have either optical radio visibility from intercepting facilities north and south. Also, Zvornik did not have radio and optical visibility of the intercepting stations north and south.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What impact does the orientation of antennas at the intercepting stations have on the possibility of intercepting certain communications?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The orientation of antennas at the intercepting stations is very important and has a great impact on the possibility of intercepting well. It can also vary. The orientation of the antennas at the radio relay stations is fixed. It is always in one fixed position, which is the best position for transmitting communications, and it is fixed by azimuth and 7 elevation. Radio relay link is a point-to-point link and it must be directed from one facility to the other as precisely as a bullet, and it must be noted that gravity does not affect the magnetic waves and they go straight. What I was able to glean from the documents of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina I looked at, they directed their antennas at the north intercepting facility, towards southeast, for some of the documents. For others, it was south. And from the southern facility, at an angle of 135 degrees and at an angle of 180 degrees. This is what was written. In my view, I believe that the antennae at the northern facility were directed at the same angles as was the south facility because north was 135 degrees and south was 180 degrees from north.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What impact does the direction of the antennas have on the possibilities of intercepting the facilities at Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Gucevo and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I analysed the situation with regard to these particular radio relay paths as contained in ABiH documents. None of the positions of the antennas were good. None of them were -- provided the best possible intercepting of communications from these facilities. As far as the orientation of the antennas of radio relay sets is concerned, their orientation was quite unfavourable for intercepting, save for two instances, and that's along the Veliki Zep and Vlasenica path, because that particular route deviates only by some 2 degrees from the direction Veliki Zep-northern intercepting facility. Which means that the northern intercepting facility was in a good position, despite the great distance from Veliki Zep, to intercept the radio-relay direction Veliki Zep-Vlasenica. The same applies to Cer-Gucevo route, which was quite appropriate for interceptions by the southern intercepting facility in terms of orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: With the antennas thus positioned, could the conversations be intercepted by the northern and southern intercepting facilities taking place in all of these radio relay stations, namely Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Gucevo, Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I did a detailed calculation for the radio relay routes Vlasenica- Veliki Zep and Zvornik-Gucevo because I had the information available with regard to frequencies at which radio relay equipment operated. I provided the findings in item 11 of the Report for RRU-800. The analysis shows that only the radio relay path between Veliki Zep and Vlasenica could have been intercepted with any quality, and the rating was good or below good. In all the other cases, the receiving signal at the intercepting stations was below the threshold normally used by the radio intercepting sets, which meant that they did not receive the signal at all, or in some cases it was just above the threshold of reception, which meant very poor reception, with a high level of noise and a very low level of intelligibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you did not analyse the possibilities of intercepting the Cer-Gucevo path?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I was unable to analyse that because the documentation of the Drina Corps did not contain the frequencies used by that particular path.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you analyse the Cer-Veliki Zep radio relay path?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I did not do that because that particular set worked in the frequency range between 4.4 to 4.6 gigahertz and 4.8 to 5 gigahertz. The BiH intercepters did not intercept these particular frequencies. At least none of the documentation I had indicated anything of the sort. In addition to that, the documentation I had at my disposal indicated that conditions were not in place that would have allowed for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify. This is the path you referred to which was maintained by?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: SMC-1306 B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suggest that we have our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. No, no. I was confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have 15 minutes more, but if you wish to have your break now, we will be very happy to grant you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not asking for an early break. I thought it was the time for the break. It was my miscalculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing while we are in an informal break, if you at any time need to put to the witness any of the diagrams, the images, appendices 18, 20 onwards, et cetera, please keep in mind, in your mind that the name of the either the north or the south location is indicated on the page and we would need either to go in private session or not have it broadcast, just to alert you to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll keep that in mind and I will decide over the break which of the options we will use. I haven't been showing our expert any of the maps or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. That's why I didn't intervene before. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I noticed that in the frequency diagram you had and which is contained in the appendices and which you say you used as the basis for your findings, there is the radio relay path Bare and Lokanj, battalion command of the 1st Bratunac Brigade, in the direction of Gucevo. I noticed that you did not take this particular path into consideration in your report. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. The document contained in appendix 13, 04314792, item 8 in the diagram of frequencies of the Drina Corps, from the month of October 1993, it is indeed there. However, in the diagram of radio relay links of the same command dated 1994 and 1995, this path cannot be found. Since I did not find it in that particular diagram, which I considered relevant, I was unable to include it in any of my calculations or in my analysis, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which frequency this particular path had in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: These were 630-megahertz and 850-megahertz frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The documents concerning intercepted conversations, did you find any conversations taking place along this path?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Seven conversations that took place on the frequency of 630 megahertz, and this was noted by the north facility. The frequency of 850 megahertz was not, however, noted down by any of the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the documents available to you, did you conclude from which location the station using 630 megahertz was?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I was able to find it in several documents, and the most relevant was the BiH army document number 0320-0963. This frequency was active from the Sarajevo area. There is mention of Lukavica, Rajlovac and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would suggest we have our break now, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are all ready to please you, Mr. Zivanovic. We'll have -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need half an hour because we are discussing matters that we will come back to you with our decision later on during the day. So it's 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Nicholls, we were wondering if you could explore the possibility of postponing the testimony of PW 128 which is scheduled -- 128, which is scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is definitely possible, Your Honour. He is not here yet. He has not flown here yet. Our view, as you know, is that it is not required, but it is possible. I do not believe that at this point we could replace him with a full witness for Monday. We would be prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not Monday. Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tuesday. Excuse me. We would be prepared to go ahead with another witness on Tuesday, I can't recall his number off-hand, I'll know it in a minute, but we could start with a witness for sure on Tuesday and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you exactly -- thank you, Judge, Judge Kwon, because that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 99, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that is possible. And then 128, he does not actually have protective measures, it's witness 128, could testify either later in the week or however Your Honours order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave that unprejudiced. Let's leave that unprejudiced. Okay. That's all we wanted to hear and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, the follow-up of all this, Mr. Nicholls, is we are minded to hand down our decision not only on the -- pursuant to the Nikolic plus Beara plus Popovic motions, not only on the interim issues or requests, but also on the substantive part of the motion as early as possible next week, but, in other words, there will be one decision dealing with both. Now, in view that you have not yet filed your response to the substantive part or substantive prayer request of Mr. Nikolic but only in relation to the request for interim provisions, you have until the -- noon on Tuesday, noon, 29, to file your response on that, if necessary, if you feel like, because that's up to you obviously, and in the meantime, the testimony of 128 will be postponed pending the determination of the whole affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That time will be sufficient. I tried to respond as much as I could in the time period, and there may be a small additional focused mainly on the law. I'm sorry. I don't quite understand, since the decision on 128 has not yet been finally reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We asked you if it could -- if it was possible for you to postpone bringing over Witness PW-128. Your answer is yes, you can replace him with someone else on Tuesday. We are kindly asking to you do so because if you don't, we would have to postpone his testimony just in case, the reason being that we, rather than deciding on the question of interim provisions only, we have decided that the two are interlinked in such a way that we need to decide both in the same decision. That will be forthcoming next week. Since we have not yet heard from you formally on your position on the substantive part, we are inviting you, if you wish so to do, to file a response, following which we will take the normal procedure and come down with our decision, which will, of course, deal with not only 108 and the 11 or 10 witnesses but also PW-128. But in the meantime, you've kindly offered to not to bring him over on Tuesday, which renders our exercise smoother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's very clear, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Dodic, many apologies to you. We needed to thrash -- Rodic, sorry, not Dodic. My apologies to you. We are going to continue dealing with something that has got absolutely nothing to do with you. My apologies to you as well, Mr. Zivanovic, for having cut through your cross-examination [sic]. Could you kindly proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I resume my cross-examination [sic], I would wish to say that we have not yet received the list of the Prosecution exhibits to be used in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of this witness. utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Vanderpuye, are there any documents that you're going to use with this witness or not, or exhibits that you're going to use?

I wasn't here at the start of the trial and was unaware of the particular decision to which my learned friend is referring, and it has been the practice, at least, that with respect to the cross-examination of the Prosecution's witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I at least have spent more than 30 years in courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't try to feed me that because there have been instances where the same criticism has been made and that included when you were cross-examining so --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have certain documents that I can certainly give a reference to. I don't know what the witness's testimony will ultimately be on direct examination, and to that extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is practice or a directive that we have exact -- that -- it's not imposed by us. It's something that you have agreed amongst ourselves, between yourselves in the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I certainly have no problem with that, Mr. President. I do recall putting on Ms. Freeze in a similar manner as this witness and I frankly didn't receive a cross-examination list of exhibits until after her final testimony which occurred over I think maybe three or four occasions, but I have no problem and I will do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.text: -- of having a problem or not having a problem. Please do it forthwith.

utterances.text: If someone can dig up the formula that we had -- you had agreed upon in the beginning of the trial, specifying the time when -- I know that there was a task imposed or agreed upon relating to a day the week before witnesses are coming over to testify. You're supposed to indicate the estimated time of -- and then I think documents, we had agreed -- yes, Madam Fauveau? Usually, your memory is --

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye and thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for having raised the issue.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the map in appendix 1, that's figure 1, and the facilities are marked on it. Could this map not be publicly broadcast because it indicates the position of the two intercepting facilities. This is Exhibit 1322, appendix 2. It's a Defence exhibit. Perhaps it might be put on the ELMO. Appendix 1. Could we zoom in a little bit, please? Mr. Rodic, if we could sharpen the focus a little bit, on this map, can you indicate the northern facility from which intercepts were made?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: It's here, elevation 815. Do I have to circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I will circle the elevation, not the symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now indicate the location of the southern facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The southern facility was at elevation 1328. [Marks]. It's this trig point here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now indicate the Vlasenica intercepting facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That is not an intercepting facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That is the terminal relay -- radio relay station where the Drina Corps command was and it's here. [Marks]. I've just circled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now indicate the Veliki Zep facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: 1537 metres above sea level. That's Veliki Zep. And it encompassed these communications and its location is right here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please mark the Cer facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The Cer facility is here at this elevation. And it encompassed these sets. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now indicate and circle the Gucevo facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Gucevo is a mountain and the peak of the mountain is called Crni Vrh, and the station was at this elevation and it included these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification, when you say Gucevo and Crni Vrh, it's one and the same facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: One and the same. Gucevo is the name of the mountain and its highest peak is called Crni Vrh. Crni Vrh is the peak of mount Gucevo and that's where the radio relay station is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which is why it's sometimes referred to as Gucevo and sometimes as Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. For the most part, it's referred to as Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please indicate the position of the Zvornik facility?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That was in Zvornik, upstream from the bridge. This is where the communication centre was. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to draw lines connecting these five facilities?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: From Vlasenica, communications went towards Veliki Zep. This is where there was a node, where telephone channels diverged and the route I analysed went this way towards Cer using an SMC device. There was another node here, then the communications went like this to Gucevo. At Gucevo, there was an interstation and then the communication went to the radio relay station in Zvornik, through the intermediate station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now indicate the RRU-800 route and the SMC route?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I will mark with 8 the RRU-800 radio relay path, with SMC –- the SMC radio relay path operated using an SMC 1306b, with 8 I mark the radio relay path operated using an RRU-800. Again with 8 I mark the radio relay path operated using an RRU-800. [Marks]. The capacity is 24 telephone channels for RRU-800 and 120 channels for the SMC. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate here the routes -- or rather I'll put that question later on. Although I might as well do so now, since we are dealing with this. Could you please mark the routes where the frequencies were known and inscribe the frequencies here?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: As I don't know this information off by heart, I will use the documentation which you also have. From Vlasenica towards Veliki Zep, the frequency was 922 megahertz. From Veliki Zep towards Vlasenica, the frequency was 680 megahertz. From Gucevo or Crni Vrh towards Zvornik, the 19 frequency was 810 megahertz. And from Zvornik towards Gucevo, 860 megahertz, 860 megahertz. There were unknown frequencies on the routes between Cer, while according to the documents of the Drina Corps, between Cer and Gucevo and between Cer and Veliki Zep, those were unknown frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now tell me, among the conditions we spoke about which might have an impact on intercepting communications, you said that the frequencies had to correspond and that was one of the prerequisites. Could you now please explain in greater detail how the matching of the frequencies between the person intercepting and the person whose communication is being intercepted is important for interception?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: When all the conditions for intercepting have been met, it is essential -- it is very important that the frequencies correspond, because the intercepting centre can listen in only on those frequencies on which communications are being transmitted between two radio relay points. So this refers to two radio relay points and one path.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now tell us how many working frequencies in total were used for communication using RRU-800 on this whole route, Vlasenica-Veliki Zep-Cer-Gucevo-Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Eight different frequencies were used, not just for RRU-800 but also for SMC, because there were four paths, and two working frequencies were needed for each path. If we exclude the frequencies for the SMC, which were within a different range, we are left with three paths using RRU-800, which makes a total of six frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now -- just a moment, please. Of all these frequencies, if I understood you correctly, four are known?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated, according to the documents of the Drina Corps, or, rather, the plan of frequencies of the Drina Corps, from October, 1993, this entire route had eight frequencies, of which four were known and they are the ones I have indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me now, were any of the communications that you analysed in the document such that they could have been intercepted on the Vlasenica-Veliki Zep path?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Because this path was operating on the frequency of 922 megahertz through 680 megahertz, and not a single one of the conversations I analysed from the documents of the BH army took place on these frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could some of the conversations you found in the documentation have been intercepted along the radio relay route Zvornik-Gucevo?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Because this radio relay path was active on the frequencies I mentioned here, 810 to 860 megahertz, and none of the frequencies noted in the ABiH documents originate or match with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you've already answered this question but for clarification sake, let's repeat it. Could any of the conversations you noted have been intercepted along the radio relay route Veliki Zep-Cer?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Because along the Veliki Zep-Cer route the SMC 1306 B radio relay set was used and the frequency range of that particular set is much higher than the one of RRU-800 and RRU-1. According to their documentation, the BiH army did not have any receivers who could -- that could intercept such conversations. In addition to that, in none of the documents I consulted did I find any indication or any annotation that would show that they had intercepted conversations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, on the Veliki Zep-Cer path, was RRU-800 used for a path?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: There was a backup route or a reserve route which was to be used in the event the SMC link is destroyed. In that case, the RRU-800 would be 6 activated and would carry the path between these two locations at the highest capacity. This particular route had been shelled in 1994, and this served 8 them as a lesson to introduce backup path which would enable them to maintain the essential services. In the document of the Drina Corps command, number 04267034, this particular path was plotted with a dotted line. Since I was a communications planner, this is done when you need to show that there should be a reserve direction on a route, and putting in place a reserve direction means that we would have to prepare the equipment at a point, at another point, to have an antenna connecter, to have an antenna, and if 15 necessary then a frequency is assigned and the direction becomes operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, does this mean that both of these paths along that route did not operate at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Precisely, because the SMC line can have the maximum of 120 channels, whereas the RRU-800 can have 24 channels. Therefore, there was a path which had a capacity that was 500 times greater and there was no need for both paths to be active along that route. While I was engaged in planning such routes, along those sections of routes that were very important, we would always, in addition to the 120-channel path, have a small-capacity backup with 24 telephone channels, in case this large-capacity link were to fail, and that is the SMC.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to your knowledge, in the summer of 1995, in the period covering the months of June, July and August, was the SMC path active or the RRU-800?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: In mid-August, 1995, when I accompanied a team to Veliki Zep, the SMC path was active and we had serviced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any previous difficulties with the operation of this particular path, let's say a month or two earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, our team was not called to intervene for that particular path. We were invited to tour all the radio relay facilities of the army of Republika Srpska. This particular visit had been planned a long time before, and we happened to be at that particular site when we visited the area in August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, out of the documentation you analysed, could any of the conversations have been intercepted according the Cer -- along the Cer-Gucevo radio relay line?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: The Cer-Gucevo path was the RRU-800 path, for which I was unable to determine the frequency. For this reason, I cannot state with any certainty whether that particular route could have been intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, tell me how many frequencies could have been there along that particular path.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Just as was the case with any relay route path, there could not have been more or less than two frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the documentation you analysed, were you able to establish how many different frequencies the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used to intercept the conversations of the army of Republika Srpska from these two particular facilities, north and south?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: My findings indicate that from the northern intercepting facility, nine different frequencies were listened into, or rather I apologise, from -- that they listened to ten frequencies. The southern intercepting facility listened in from ten different frequencies. Four frequencies were used by both facilities. If we take both of these intercepting facilities into consideration, then the documents were produced on 16 different frequencies, as was in fact indicated in the BH army documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From these two unknown frequencies, could all these conversations have been intercepted, all 16 or nine or 10 conversations?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: They could have been listened to only on two frequencies along this particular route.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that only under the condition that some of these intercepts --

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: On condition that the conversations intercepted corresponded to the conversations that were transmitted along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If none of these conversations that were noted down originated from either of these frequencies, what would your finding be?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: My finding would be that there was no possibility of intercepting any of the conversations contained in the BH army documents with the matching -- or with these particular frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in addition to the five facilities we mentioned, namely Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Gucevo and Zvornik, were interceptions with RRU-800 could have been -- or rather were they taken or could they have been taken from some other facilities?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Judging on the principle of operation of radio relay links, that would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What we gave you was something that we were given by the Prosecution, and that was the plan of frequency of 1993. That plan of frequencies dating from 1993, was it modified in the subsequent period until 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: That sort of plan of frequencies, based on a stationary system, is modified very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And why is that the case? Why is it not frequently changed?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: I have experience in that field since I participated in the modifications of such plans. This is a complex job which calls for the modification of frequencies throughout the territory covered by an army, in this case throughout Republika Srpska. In technological terms it is quite complex and in this case it would have called for the harmonisation and changes in the plan of frequencies in western Serbia. Moreover, in my view, such modifications were not necessary. The normal voice information could have been conveyed this way. Where necessary, confident -- or rather, when it was necessary to convey confidential information, they were transmitted in coded, encrypted telegrams as was normally the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, can you please place your signature and today's date on the map you have before you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Are there any additional questions that any one of the other Defence teams who have engaged Mr. Rodic wish to make to him, wish to put to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same here, Your Honour. We will not have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nor do we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I will only seek some clarification from expert Rodic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rodic, concerning your expert report, can you explain the notion of a radio relay link in greater detail to me as a layman?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: It is quite difficult to put it briefly. Perhaps I may be allowed to sketch a simple diagram or to show you a simple diagram to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Which diagram is that?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No. This diagram is not contained in the report but I would like to use one to explain this to you. Or I can use appendix 18 to explain in greater detail the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any problem with anyone with the witness using the diagram that he has in his hands? None? Okay. Go ahead. Mr. Rodic, you can use the diagram that you were -- you had in your hand a minute ago. Thank you. There is no names on that diagrams, no? Of locations or anything? Mr. Rodic, there are no names of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very general and there are no specific names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A radio relay link is a sublink to radio links. It is different from a radio communication because it is a point-to-point radio link. Let us look at the diagram. Between this particular facility here and the other one there, there exists a radio relay link. This symbol means that RRU-800 is used, which can carry up to 24 telephone channels. It does not contain a multiplex facility, which is why the multiplex facility is added here. It has not been so important for this analysis because it does not transmit frequencies. It only facilitates the passage of signals along the relay route. What this stands for is a radio channel in the frequency range of 03 to 4 kilohertz. The multiplex facility enables the 24 channels to be combined into RRU-800, which are then transmitted along the route to the other station. At the other station, there is a similar multiplex which splits the signal into individual channels so that at the end of the story we have 24 telephone channels here, and they are presented here. Let us now use diagram 18 from the document here to explain to you in technical terms how this particular link was established and with the use of which devices, if you'll allow me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before that, can you please place your signature and today's date on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do you have elements for a radio link on this diagram to explain to us?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: No. That was not part of my analysis. I only said that this was one type of a radio link. I simply wanted to state that this particular link is a directed, point-to-point communication which is very important for the interception of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that if one wishes to hear the participants in a conversation, there must not exist a single obstacle between these two points?

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: According to the regulations governing radio relaying, there must not be a single physical obstacle along not only the route that was plotted here but between the two points, there has to be what I called radio visibility. This means that below this particular line drawn here, there must not be any obstacles such as mountains and so on and so forth. This is the principle governing radio relaying. The energy between these two points is transmitted as an ellipsoid. The area within the ellipsoid must be free. This is called the first Frenel [phoen] zone, a free zone. This term is contained in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, before we move on to diagram or figure 18, let us go back to appendix 1 or -- yes, appendix 1, which was used in Mr. Zivanovic's examination.

utterances.speaker: DJURO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it on my monitor. I don't know if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
